chapter: Struttin' Time, chronology and Chicago singers
title: Never in the Blackbirds; Sissle's color prejudice
summary: She worked for Lou Leslie once, but Eubie Blake's shows never took her because Sissle or his fair wife preferred light skin and thought blues beneath him.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yes, did you ever work -- you worked for Lou Leslie?
I worked for Lou Leslie. What did I do for him? Something I did for Lou Leslie. He sent me someplace. I don't recall where.
You were never in any of the Blackbirds?

No, I tell you what. Eubie Blake wanted me many times in his shows, but Sissle was partial to color. He was married to a girl who was very fair, and I don't know whether it was Sissle who was fair -- who was partial to color or Harriet, his wife, and, however, and Sissle thought that to sing the blues was, you know, down to the --
-- beneath him, beneath him, but Eubie Blake was always wonderful and kind to everybody. Now, he had me --
